issues: The lead's second paragraph calls Miatta Fahnbulleh 'the UK's climate minister', but both the ORIGINAL and the REWRITE's own body text identify her as 'the UK's energy minister' — a title mismatch within the same piece.
The march on the presidency is described twice (once in the new lead paragraph, once again later in the body at its original position) — mildly repetitive but not a hard violation.

The added progress-line paragraph ('Police have charged a man with attempted murder, assault and possessing an offensive weapon; he appeared in court on Saturday and is due back on 21 December.') is pure procedural restatement of facts already in the standfirst and adds nothing hopeful or forward-looking. The family's own quote ('grateful for the overwhelming kindness shown and hopes to personally thank everyone once he has recovered'), already in the body, would have made a genuine progress beat but was not used there.

The progress line says Prinsley 'is pushing for' asylum seekers to be housed in cities instead, but the ORIGINAL only reports he 'suggested' this 'may be more appropriate' — a stronger, more active claim of campaigning than the source supports.

The progress line states environmental protections 'may yet block' the development, but the ORIGINAL only says planning permission 'may be difficult to attain' and any application would be 'very difficult' — it never says the project would be blocked.

The added progress line claims 'Players say... [Moody] helped inspire their performance by joining the pre-match haka.' No player is quoted anywhere in the ORIGINAL making this causal claim; the original only describes the moment as symbolically powerful and links to a separately-titled related article calling Moody 'inspirational'. Attributing a specific claim about inspiring the performance to unnamed 'players' is not supported by the source text.

The headline and progress line credit an unreported response ('Players say... helped inspire their performance') — no such player quote exists in the source, so this invents a feel-good causal narrative rather than reporting one.

The third line ('Negotiators have produced a new draft text aimed at resolving the impasse over the phaseout.') is a near-verbatim restatement of the headline ('issue fresh draft text to break... deadlock') and adds no new information.

The headline settles for a thin procedural development (a new draft text) when the fuller story offers a more concrete, human angle — nations marching on the summit presidency to demand reinstatement of the pledge — that this preview does not use.

Headline and both follow-on lines stay purely procedural ('Police lay three charges...', 'Police have charged a 31-year-old man...') — essentially a cosmetic rewording of the same charge-focused angle as the original, with no reframing toward any upside.

The fuller article version of this same story leads with a genuine upside (the councillor is stable after heroically protecting a colleague), but this preview ignores that entirely, leaving only violent charge detail with no sense of recovery.
The third line duplicates charge information already given twice (headline and standfirst), adding nothing new.

The progress line ('The local MP has publicly pushed back against attempts to use the vote to stir up racial discord.') restates the headline and standfirst's claim about the MP opposing racial discord for a third time, adding no new information.

Cosmetic edit — the headline swaps 'helps sparkling England power to' for 'sparks England to' and 'wilt again' for 'faltering', keeping exactly the same subject and angle as the original with no substantive change.

The third line ('The US justice department has charged the group responsible for the burglaries.') is a near-verbatim restatement of both the headline and the standfirst, which already say the same thing — it adds no new information.

The progress line ('...say they are seeing real change in how victims are treated by the justice system') largely restates the headline's own claim ('things are really changing'), adding little beyond what the headline already says — a weaker example of the redundant-progress-line pattern seen elsewhere in this batch, though the rest of the piece (headline and standfirst) is strong and well-grounded in the two best quotes.

Cosmetic edit — 'insiders' becomes 'staff who have left' and 'cuts' becomes 'cost-cutting', but the headline and standfirst retain exactly the same critical angle with no substantive change. (The underlying story may genuinely have no available upside, but a pointless word-swap is not the same as a deliberate, calm non-edit.)

Cosmetic edit — the headline just inverts the same sentence ('Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break... turnover' becomes 'New Manager Bounce is... route out of... turnover cycle') without any substantive change in framing or information.

Headline and standfirst are completely unchanged from the original and still lead with the setback ('Fragile... must toughen up... Leeds humiliation') with no reframing toward any upside and no silver lining anywhere in the copy. For a second-pass revision this looks like no fix was applied at all.
Cosmetic edit — 'thwarted by Liverpool keeper' becomes 'held by brilliant Keating' and 'move to third' becomes 'climb to third'; same facts and angle with only decorative wording changes.

The headline softens the critic's pointed original argument ('is an insult to objective truth') into a milder complaint ('needed more hard facts'). The direction of the argument is preserved rather than reversed, so this is acceptable, but it blunts the opinion writer's force more than a straight 'rephrase forward' should.
Cosmetic edit on an already-positive headline — 'arrested in special forces raid' becomes 'capture... after decade-long manhunt'; the same angle restated with no substantive change.

Standfirst changes 'more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday' to 'predicted to fall...by Sunday' — this shifts the claim from rain falling specifically on Sunday to a cumulative total reached by Sunday, a real change in the timing/meaning of the forecast, not just wording.

Added final line 'The CBO is pressing for more realistic cost estimates on the new warship programme' asserts an ongoing advocacy action by the CBO that is not stated in the original — the original only says the CBO 'finds' the estimated cost 'unrealistically low', not that it is actively pressing for anything.

The revision is still a cosmetic reshuffle of the same bad-news story (cost overruns, stretched capacity) with no genuine upside — reframing it around 'watchdog scrutiny' doesn't change that this is fundamentally the same setback, and the added third line is a vague, invented-sounding 'progress' statement (CBO 'pressing for' reform) that isn't actually reported in the original, which is exactly the kind of unreported-response problem a prior review should have caught.

This is a cosmetic edit: 'Haitians excited but uneasy' became 'troops draw welcome and worry' — same subject, same dual-sided framing, same order (positive word first, then the worry), just synonym-swapped. No new angle or genuine additional upside was introduced; this is the pattern a second pass should flag as not actually fixed.

Standfirst adds 'but experts say closing that gap is only a matter of time' — the original only says 'Experts are racing to change that', i.e. they are trying, with no stated view on how close they are or on what timeline. Asserting that closing the dexterity gap is 'only a matter of time' is an invented degree of certainty/optimism not supported by the original.

The added claim that closing the robotic-hand gap is 'only a matter of time' credits experts with a confident, unreported prediction (criterion 8) to manufacture an upside — a fabricated optimistic claim is not a legitimate fix, even though dropping the 'doom of humanity' framing was itself a reasonable move.
Cosmetic swap only: 'criticised over safety fears' becomes 'urge caution' for the same story with no new angle or genuine upside.

The added third line ('Experts are urging caution about BBL and other cosmetic procedures sold in Black Friday deals') is a near-verbatim restatement of the headline/standfirst, not real additional progress information — exactly the vague-restatement problem the brief flags under criterion 8.

The headline paraphrase changes the meaning of the original joke: the original says 'Calling it thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry' (i.e. even the insult of calling it thin gruel would be too kind, an insult to gruel itself). The rewrite's headline, 'a dead-eyed advert that insults the gruel industry', drops the thin-gruel comparison and asserts the advert itself directly insults the gruel industry — a different, flattened claim attributed as if it were the original's point.

Added third line claims small-business owners are stepping in 'across England' — the given original text never specifies England as the scope; this is an added geographic claim not supported by the text being checked against.

The added third line just restates the headline/standfirst ('small-business owners...stepping in to sponsor...teams' vs '...stepping in to sponsor their local teams') without adding any real new progress information — a vague restatement under criterion 8, and it also introduces the unsupported 'across England' claim flagged in the fact check.

Headline 'Calls grow to protect teenagers in law' asserts the campaign is growing/escalating — the original only says campaigners 'call for changes to the law on consent', with no stated claim about the calls increasing over time. This adds an unsupported momentum claim.

The verification status is inverted. The original headline states as settled that 'Two groups verify mathematician's claim' (verification presented as having occurred), while the rewrite downgrades this to 'with two groups now verifying his claim' (present continuous, i.e. verification still in progress) — while simultaneously upgrading the headline itself to assert flatly that 'Claude helps mathematician solve' the hypothesis, as settled fact. This swaps which part of the story is certain and which is still pending, which matters a great deal for a claim about solving the Riemann hypothesis.
The rewrite drops the specific start day: the original standfirst says talks 'begin on Monday', while the rewrite's standfirst only says talks 'begin' with no day given.

Headline claims negotiators got the early draft text 'to speed search for deal' — the original attributes a different purpose to the president of the talks: the draft is an attempt to 'draw out parties' (get them to reveal where they stand), and frames the early delivery as something that surprised many countries, not as a deliberate speed-up tactic. Presenting it as designed to 'speed' the deal is an invented characterization of intent.

The 'genuine upside' in this headline — that the early draft is meant to speed up the search for a deal — is manufactured rather than reported; the original frames the early draft as a surprise and a device to draw out positions, not a confirmed accelerant. Building the headline on an invented positive spin is the kind of unreported-response problem criterion 8 warns against.

Headline says the sister 'recovers' (completed action) while the original says she is 'recovering' (ongoing, present status only) — this overstates the outcome as resolved when the original only confirms she was, at time of writing, in the process of recovering.

The 'Justice delivered:' headline tag is a triumphant, editorializing flourish bolted onto a story about the murder of a woman and three children. A serious British paper would state the sentence plainly (as the original does) rather than brand a multiple-child-killing case with a celebratory label — this reads as reaching for an upside angle at the expense of appropriate gravity, bordering on the kind of tonal overcorrection a second pass should catch.

Headline's 'remembered for a much-loved career' asserts an active process of commemoration/tribute that is not stated in the ORIGINAL, which only reports the death and his roles — this is an added, unsupported characterization.

Headline drops the death entirely (no 'dies'/'has died') and replaces it with the soft, vague 'remembered for a much-loved career', which minimises the death by removing it from the headline — a direct violation of rule 5, even though the standfirst does separately state 'has died aged 77'.
'Remembered for a much-loved career' is a consoling, eulogy-style phrase that risks breaking voice for a straight news obituary item rather than re-stating the facts plainly.

Headline turns the ORIGINAL's own prescriptive statement ('but England must play with freedom', the writer's assessment) into passive reported speech ('England told to play with freedom'), implying an unnamed outside party instructed them to do so — an attribution not present in, or supported by, the ORIGINAL.

Headline attributes 'discipline and bench impact will decide' the game to Maro Itoje ('Itoje says...'), but in the ORIGINAL only the description of the game as a 'massive game' is Itoje's quote; the claim that discipline and bench impact will be pivotal is the writer's own framing, not something Itoje is reported as saying — this misattributes analysis to a named person.
Drops 'the breakdown' from the three factors ('discipline, bench impact and the breakdown') the ORIGINAL says will be pivotal, leaving only two.

Cosmetic edit: same subject/angle as the ORIGINAL (district attorneys suing/challenging Newsom's clemency) with swapped wording ('sue to stop' → 'challenge'); it does not foreground any upside (e.g. the clemency/mercy itself, which could be the genuine upside here) and leaves the opposition-led framing essentially intact.

ORIGINAL headline quotes the protester's message as addressed to three companies — OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta. REWRITE headline addresses the message to only 'OpenAI and Meta', dropping Anthropic — changing who the quoted message was for.

ORIGINAL says the operation 'wards off risk of cyber-attack' — a vulnerability was closed pre-emptively; no actual attack occurred. REWRITE says cyber defenders 'head off attack' on the fridges and freezers, implying an actual attack was underway and was stopped — a stronger and different claim than merely heading off a risk.
